title: Debt Avalanche vs Snowball: Which Method Is Better?
seoTitle: Debt Avalanche vs Snowball Method: Which Saves More?
excerpt: How the two most popular debt payoff methods work, a worked example, and how to choose.
description: The debt avalanche and debt snowball methods compared: how each one works, a worked example with real numbers, and how to choose the right one for you.
body:
If you have more than one debt, the order you pay them off in matters. The two most popular methods are the debt avalanche and the debt snowball. Both start the same way: pay the minimum on every debt, then put every spare pound towards one target debt.

## The debt avalanche

You target the debt with the **highest interest rate** first. When it's paid off, its payment moves to the debt with the next highest rate, and so on.

- **Pro:** it usually costs the least interest overall
- **Con:** if your highest-rate debt is also large, it can take a while to see your first debt disappear

## The debt snowball

You target the **smallest balance** first, whatever its interest rate. Each debt you clear frees up its payment for the next smallest. The method was popularised by the US radio host Dave Ramsey.

- **Pro:** quick early wins, which helps many people stay motivated
- **Con:** it can cost more interest, because a high-rate debt may wait in the queue

## A worked example

Here are three debts, with £100 a month extra on top of the minimum payments:

- Credit card: £3,500 at 29.9% APR, minimum £105
- Car loan: £6,000 at 7.9% APR, minimum £180
- Store card: £800 at 19.9% APR, minimum £25

Using our [debt payoff calculator](/tools/debt-payoff-calculator/):

- **Avalanche** pays off the credit card first, then the store card, then the car loan. Total interest: about £2,114.
- **Snowball** pays off the store card first, then the credit card, then the car loan. Total interest: about £2,259.

Both clear everything in 2 years 7 months here, but the avalanche saves about £145. Without the extra £100 a month, it would take about 4 years and cost around £4,345 in interest. The extra payment matters far more than the method.

## Which should you choose?

- **Choose the avalanche** if your interest rates are very different and you're motivated by saving the most money.
- **Choose the snowball** if you've struggled to stick with a plan before and quick wins would keep you going.
- **Either is far better than paying only the minimums.** The most important thing is to pick one and stick with it.

## Tips that work with both methods

- Never miss a minimum payment: fees and missed-payment markers make things worse
- Put windfalls such as bonuses or tax refunds towards your target debt
- Find spare money for extra payments with the [50/30/20 budget calculator](/tools/budget-calculator/)
- If your debts feel unmanageable, speak to a free, independent debt advice service

Add your own debts to the free [debt payoff calculator](/tools/debt-payoff-calculator/) to see both methods side by side. BudgetWise also has a debt payoff planner with both methods built in.
